extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary criticism; literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for doing systematic literary criticism oriented around archetypes, myth, ritual, and genre; explains methods (structural, inductive/deductive), central myths (the quest), and comic/tragic imagery patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism as a systematic science (assumption of total coherence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first postulate: criticism can be a 'totally intelligible' organized body of knowledge; assume total coherence in the science of criticism even if literature itself is inexhaustible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat criticism like a developing science: seek organizing principles or a 'central hypothesis' that will allow progressive learning and cumulative knowledge rather than leisure-class conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish criticism from literature (teachability criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot 'learn literature' in the direct sense; what can be taught and learned is the criticism of literature—the systematic study about literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame pedagogical goals around teaching methods of criticism (evidence, textual editing, prosody, philology) rather than attempting to 'teach' literature as a direct experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude meaningless or pseudo-propositional criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaningless criticism is talking about literature in a way that cannot help build a systematic structure of knowledge; 'pseudo-propositions' and casual value-judgments are to be recognized and discarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sentimental judgments, judgments based on religious or political prejudice, and leisure-class conversational pronouncements; prioritize statements that contribute to systematic knowledge and that are based on literary experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreground structural (rhetorical) analysis as initial critical effort
rubrics_metrics.description: The first effort of critical apprehension should take the form of a rhetorical or structural analysis of a work of art: narrative as linear movement; meaning as the integrity of the completed form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use close textual work (editing, prosody, rhetoric) to establish the centripetal perspective, but remember its limits and relation to larger principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance inductive and deductive procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceed inductively from structural analysis to see larger patterns, and deductively by postulating unity; neither pure induction nor pure deduction is sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use iterative correction between data-driven generalization and theory-driven deduction to avoid haphazard guessing or rigid pigeon-holing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse causes: efficient, formal, and material
rubrics_metrics.description: A work's unity involves efficient cause (artist) and formal cause (form/genre); inquire also into material cause (social conditions and cultural demands that produced a genre).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine literary psychology (connect poet and poem), genre analysis (formal cause), and literary history/social context (material cause) in a coordinated critical approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use literary psychology judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic needs a kind of literary psychology connecting the poet with the poem; biographical psychological study is useful chiefly in analysing failures and private mythologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply psychological analysis where it illuminates expression or failure, but situate character-psychology within literary conventions rather than treating it as the primary explanatory framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid naive conceptions of genre (neither Platonic nor purely biological)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres are not preexistent fixed forms (pseudo‑Platonic) nor merely evolving biological species; truth lies between these extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat genre as a product of formal and material conditions—use genre categories cautiously and historically, not as immutable essences or linear evolutionary stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ literary anthropology: seek archetypes in ritual, myth, folktale
rubrics_metrics.description: The search for archetypes is 'a kind of literary anthropology'—look to pre-literary categories (ritual, myth, folktale) to explain recurrent literary structures and imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study ritualic, mythic, and folktale formulas as sources or recurring patterns that grand literature reverts to; treat anthropology and psychology as relevant allied sciences, but allow criticism its autonomous aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multi-level 'step-back' analysis from text to archetype
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding proceeds by successive steps outward: textual editing → rhetoric/philology → literary psychology → genre/context → archetype; each step gives a different vantage on meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting a scene or symbol, 'back up' progressively to see psychological networks, genre placement, and finally archetypal forms; assemble converging scholarly interests under a central critical pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the quest-myth as the central narrative myth
rubrics_metrics.description: Frye identifies the central myth of literature as the quest-myth, which structures narratives and can be seen in four cyclical phases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the quest-myth as a unifying logical derivation for genre relations (epic, lyric, drama, etc.), but avoid chronological prehistory; treat the derivation as a deductive classification within criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quest-myth phase 1: dawn/spring/birth (romance archetype)
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths of the birth of the hero, revival and resurrection, creation, and the defeat of darkness; subordinate characters: the father and the mother; archetype of romance and dithyrambic/rhapsodic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize motifs of birth/rebirth and their placement in romance and exuberant poetic forms when classifying works within the cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quest-myth phase 2: zenith/summer/marriage/triumph (comedy archetype)
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths of apotheosis, the sacred marriage, and entering Paradise; subordinate characters: the companion and the bride; archetype of comedy, pastoral and idyll.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify images of triumph, consummation, and communal harmony as signaling the comic/pastoral phase in a work's archetypal mapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quest-myth phase 3: sunset/autumn/death (tragedy archetype)
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths of fall, the dying god, violent death and sacrifice, isolation of the hero; subordinate characters: the traitor and the siren; archetype of tragedy and elegy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map motifs of decline, sacrifice, and isolation to the tragic/elegiac strand in the overarching mythic cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quest-myth phase 4: darkness/winter/dissolution (satire archetype)
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths of the triumph of powers of darkness, floods, return of chaos, defeat of the hero (Gotterdammerung); subordinate characters: the ogre and the witch; archetype of satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See themes of dissolution, chaos, and the dominance of destructive forces as the darkest phase, often expressed satirically or catastrophically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish rhythm (narrative) from pattern (meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm (temporal recurrence) corresponds to narrative; pattern (spatial recurrence) corresponds to simultaneous grasp of verbal structure or meaning. Literature lies between music (rhythm) and painting (pattern).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze a work both as linear movement (narrative sequence) and as a total pattern (meaning/integrity); experimental writing often pushes toward either boundary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of narrative in ritual; imagery from epiphany/oracle
rubrics_metrics.description: Ritual (temporal sequence of acts) tends toward narrative origin; patterns/fragments of significance derive from epiphanic/oracular moments which build encyclopedic doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace narrative structures to ritual context and imagistic patterns to moments of revelation—this explains why both tend to become encyclopedic in higher cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth as the archetype: solar/seasonal/human cycles inform imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Myth constitutes the archetype, constructing central narratives and patterns of significance (e.g., the solar cycle producing hero-figures who are part sun/vegetative/fertility/god).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study sacred scriptures and canonical myths as primary documents for archetypal criticism because they instantiate the central encyclopedic myth-structures critics must understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat divine/epiphany as human/artistic phenomena (stance toward religious content)
rubrics_metrics.description: In criticism the divine is treated as a character in a human story; epiphanies are explained as mental phenomena linked to dreams; art deals with the conceivable, not the actual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics need not adopt religious belief; instead analyse divine figures and epiphanies as literary constructs within human imaginative structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of identity between individual and universal image forms
rubrics_metrics.description: An essential principle of archetypal criticism is that the individual and the universal forms of an image are identical (the reasons are complex but this underlies the method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this principle to justify reading single images both as unique instances and as manifestations of universal archetypal patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vs. tragic vision — human world imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic vision: human world as a community (symposium, communion, friendship, love); tragic vision: human world as tyranny/anarchy or isolated individual (deserted/betrayed hero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret social and relational imagery (marriage, community vs betrayal, isolation) according to the comic or tragic context to determine tonal alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vs. tragic vision — animal world imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic: community of domesticated animals (flock, lamb, dove); Tragic: beasts/birds of prey (wolves, vultures, serpents, dragons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use animal imagery to signal pastoral/comic or predatory/tragic contexts in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vs. tragic vision — vegetable world imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic: garden, grove, park, tree of life, rose or lotus (Arcadian images); Tragic: sinister forest, heath, wilderness, tree of death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess plant/landscape imagery for signs of Arcadian/community or hostile/desolating significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vs. tragic vision — mineral/world/city imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic: city, temple, glowing precious stone, luminous geometrical images (starlit dome); Tragic: deserts, rocks, ruins, sinister geometrical images such as the cross.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read built-environment and mineral imagery for whether they connote ordered civic/comic vision or ruinous/tragic desolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic vs. tragic vision — unformed world imagery (river/sea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic: unformed world as river (fourfold, temperate, life-giving); Tragic: as the sea (flood, dissolution) often producing leviathan and water-monsters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret water imagery (river vs sea) as indicative of life-sustaining/comic or dissolving/tragic mythic contexts.
